partial_progress.details: Phases 1-4 of 11 complete and committed cleanly (depth-first, one phase closed before the next opened). Phases 1-2 landed the independently-landable Gate 8 finding-extraction fix and its 13-site generalization. Phase 3 built an idle-guarded cost-measurement harness and captured a clean 23-gate cost table. Phase 4 introduced the declarative gate registry and migrated gates 1-8 with proven byte-identical output. Pausing at this clean phase boundary rather than opening Phase 5 (a comparable-or-larger scope: migrate gates 9-23, add cost-class selection, re-verify 5 deploy_findings_snapshot callers, full-battery before/after capture) given the real-world time already spent on this dispatch (multiple multi-minute background waits for idle-load windows and full-battery measurements, including live contention spikes to load 50+ from concurrent sibling /orchestrate sessions).

memory_candidates.content: IFS=$'\t' read -r a b c ... silently collapses a genuinely EMPTY field between two tabs in a TSV row, shifting every later column by one -- bash classifies tab as an IFS-whitespace character even when it is IFS's sole member, so consecutive-delimiter sequences (which an empty field produces) are treated the same as leading/trailing whitespace stripping and silently merged. This is NOT specific to tab -- any IFS value consisting entirely of whitespace-class characters (space, tab, newline) has this behavior; only a non-whitespace single-char delimiter (comma, pipe) reliably preserves empty fields under plain `read`. Fix: use a placeholder token (e.g. '-') for an intentionally-empty TSV field, and normalize it back to empty string after the read, rather than emitting a bare empty field between two tabs.

When extracting N copy-pasted bash blocks into named functions for a declarative-dispatch refactor, inserting the function DEFINITIONS section immediately adjacent to (just before) the blocks' own original textual position -- rather than relocating them to a logically-organized-but-distant new location (e.g. top of file) -- keeps the diff minimal and easy to review: git's diff recognizes the largely-unchanged body text as context rather than wholesale delete+add, even though the surrounding control flow (an if/fi wrapper replaced by a loop) did change. This made an 8-gate, ~340-line extraction show as a ~55-line diff instead of a full-file rewrite, and made a byte-identical-output verification trivial to trust by inspection as well as by diff.
